title: What Data from 20m Pull Requests Reveal About AI Transformation — Nick Arcolano, Jellyfish
talk_summary: Jellyfish analyzed ~20M PRs across ~1000 companies and found AI adoption correlates with ~2x PR throughput and ~24% faster cycle time, with PRs ~18% larger but no statistically significant quality degradation. The key moderator is code architecture: teams with centralized/balanced repos see ~4x gains, while highly distributed repos show essentially no correlation, attributed to cross-repo context being hard for tools and agents.

takeaways.technique: Consolidate repo topology / write down cross-repo relationships
takeaways.what_they_do: They segment companies by 'active repos per engineer' and find AI productivity gains collapse in highly distributed architectures because tools work one repo at a time and inter-repo relationships live only in senior engineers' heads.
takeaways.evidence_quote: combining context across repos, it's often challenging. It's challenging uh for humans as well as for coding tools and for agents
takeaways.numbers: centralized/balanced ~4x PR throughput gain vs ~2x global average; highly distributed ~0 (slightly negative)

takeaways.technique: Track change in PR throughput and cycle time as productivity metrics, not absolute counts
takeaways.what_they_do: They explicitly warn that absolute PR counts vary with architecture (distributed repos need more PRs for migrations/coordination) and recommend measuring the change in throughput and cycle time (first commit→merge) instead.
takeaways.evidence_quote: counting PRs in the absolute sense isn't isn't a great metric. You really need to be tracking change in PR throughput
takeaways.numbers: ~2x PR throughput; ~24% cycle-time decrease at full adoption

takeaways.technique: Calibrate review anxiety against bug/revert rates
takeaways.what_they_do: They looked at bug tickets created and PR revert rates and found no statistically significant relationship with AI adoption rate, suggesting quality fears may be overblown relative to throughput gains.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we haven't found any statistically significant relationship with the rate of AI adoption
takeaways.numbers: no statistically significant effect on bug tickets or reverts

takeaways.technique: Route well-scoped bug tickets to agents first
takeaways.what_they_do: They observe teams disproportionately use AI on bug tickets because bugs are well-scoped, verifiable tasks, driving up bug-resolution rates without increasing bug creation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: bugs are often well scoped verifiable tasks that AI coding tools can be set up well to succeed at
takeaways.numbers: increased rates of bugs resolved, attributed to AI tackling backlog bug tickets

takeaways.technique: Expect bigger PRs from AI and size review/CI accordingly
takeaways.what_they_do: They measured that fully-adopted teams push PRs ~18% larger in net lines added, mostly additions within the same files rather than touching more files.
takeaways.evidence_quote: teams that have fully adopted AI coding tools are pushing PRs that are 18% larger in terms of net lines of code added
takeaways.numbers: ~18% larger PRs; number of files touched roughly unchanged
